newsitem.title: USA: Dollar surges above 122 yen to set fresh 4-year high.
newsitem.headline: Dollar surges above 122 yen to set fresh 4-year high.

text.p: The dollar vaulted to its highest level against the yen in just under four years Wednesday, buoyed by a growing sense that Japan is willing to tolerate persistent weakness in its currency.

Remarks from a Japanese official, which suggested Japan is unlikely to actively defend the yen soon, and another day of sharp gains in Japanese stocks both contributed to the perception that Japan has no urgent desire or need to reverse yen weakness, dealers said.
Against the mark, the dollar retreated, ending modestly weaker after Germany's head central banker said the dollar's rise against the mark was nearing an end.

The dollar ended the day at 122.13 yen, up from 121.00 at Tuesday's close. It touched a peak of 122.75 yen, its highest level since early February of 1993, in Asian trade. The dollar closed at 1.6440 marks, below Tuesday's close of 1.6480.
The dollar's gains against the yen were curbed earlier in the week by fears that Japan's central bank would sell dollars for yen in the foreign exchange markets to boost its currency.

But Wednesday, Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said that "calling for stable currencies could lead to stability itself," a sign to many in the market that Japan is likely to continue to use rhetoric rather than active currency intervention to curb excessive yen weakness.
The pressure on Japan to defend the yen was also alleviated by more gains in Japanese stocks, traders said.

The Nikkei average of 225 leading Japanese shares, which has slumped badly in recent months prompting concerns about weakness in the yen, jumped over 530 points on Wednesday after rising some 461 points Tuesday.

"As the domestic Japanese markets stabilise, I think the perception is that there will be less pressure on the Japanese to defend the yen," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago.

The dollar's lackluster performance against European currencies was linked to remarks from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, who predicted an end to the dollar's rise from 1995's post-World War II lows against the mark.
The German central bank chief said Wednesday that he expected the "normalization" of the mark's exchange rate against the dollar to end soon, prompting a flood of dollar sales.

"Tietmeyer's comments were a key development," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "People used them as an excuse to sell the dollar against the mark and other European currencies."

Elsewhere, the dollar ended modestly weaker at 1.4260 Swiss francs against 1.4275 on Tuesday, despite remarks from the chairman of the Swiss central bank that the weakening franc was helping the struggling Swiss economy.
Sterling ended modestly stronger at $1.6207 versus $1.6175 on Tuesday. The dollar advanced to Canadian $1.3455 against C$1.3400.
